articles.title: ‘You have a meeting’: the calendar phishing scam growing exponentially
articles.summary: Appointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal page. You’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at your Google calendar. There’s an entry for a meeting that you must have completely forgotten.
body: Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they are contacting you from your bank, or another institution.
Luke Wescott, a threat detection engineer at Sublime Security, says calendar phishing is still relatively new but the company has seen “exponential growth”.
The scam takes several forms, including a fake meeting, or a prompt to renew a service you pay for. In all, an entry appears in your electronic calendar.
It ends up there after scammers send an email to your work, or personal address, with a calendar request. It doesn’t matter if you miss it, or it ends up in your spam folder.

articles.title: How the 2026 Super El Niño and Climate Change Are Related
articles.summary: Here’s what we know about the record-setting El Niño on a record-hot planet, and the most important questions scientists are trying to answer.
body: The tropical Pacific has seen heat build for months as a “super” El Niño takes shape.

A climate phenomenon that forms every few years, this year’s iteration of El Niño has been on a tear of daily records and is forecast to reach unprecedented strength this winter. While it’s characterized by hotter-than-normal waters in the eastern tropical Pacific, El Niño is a global problem.

It’s fair to wonder how another global problem is interacting with El Niño: climate change, driven by burning fossil fuels. While a hotter climate begetting a hotter El Niño might seem like a done deal, “I have more questions than I have reactions” to what’s happening, says Christopher Callahan, a climate researcher at Indiana University. In other words, the relationship is still an area of active research—and this year’s event could provide vital insights.

El Niño’s added ocean heat affects the atmosphere causing weather patterns around the world shift. Consider it kind of like a domino run, where one tile starts a chain reaction. Such a major slug of heat in the Pacific will act more like a shove then a light flick on the atmosphere, and the resulting shifts in weather expected to be generationally intense.

articles.title: California’s Tallest and Most Iconic Trees Are Getting Heatstroke
articles.summary: Redwoods adapted to a cool, foggy climate. Now a new study shows they slow down photosynthesis when their environment warms.
body: This story originally appeared on Vox and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A grove of coast redwood trees is a forest of forests. Individual trees can live for thousands of years, and as they grow, their canopies develop mats of soils and ferns, creating something like a second forest floor hundreds of feet above the ground.

These elevated ecosystems are home to creatures like the wandering salamander, which can spend its entire life cycle on top of a single tree, and the marbled murrelet, a seabird whose nesting habits were a mystery until one day in 1974, when a tree-trimmer stumbled upon a nest 150 feet above the ground. Sometimes a stray seed—a sitka spruce or oak or even another redwood—finds its way up a massive redwood and grows into another tree entirely, nestled among the branches of a giant.
points: Now a new study shows they slow down photosynthesis when their environment warms.

articles.title: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessment
articles.summary: Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists. Humans could become extinct by the year 2100 due to malicious use of AI or nuclear conflict, according to a new global risk assessment.
body: They top a list of 17 major threats to human health over the next 75 years, which also includes cuts to aid spending by wealthy countries, the climate crisis and childhood malnutrition.

The experts behind The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health said all the threats interact, meaning they must be addressed together – but stressed that there was “a realistic route to act” on each.

“Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” said Prof Christopher Murray, commission co-chair and the director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington.

To create its list, the commission modelled how many years in good health might be lost due to sickness, disability or early deaths due to each threat, based on current trajectories – a measure known as disability-adjusted life years (Dalys).

articles.title: Parents fear YouTubers are bringing ‘brain rot’ to Netflix. But are kids wising up to ‘slop’?
articles.summary: As streamers poach viral creators to appeal to children, digital whack-a-mole has become a new kind of family challenge. Exasperated dad Simon Hooper shakes his fist at the camera in a viral video.
body: The precise “brain rot” he’s referring to is the arrival of a polarising show that’s lighting up parent chats around the globe. And while Salish and Jordan Matter might be new to Netflix Kids users, the father-daughter content creators are familiar to anyone who’s spent any time on the internet.

Think gamified family life challenges such as “ I Went On a Fake Date To Prank My Dad ” and “ I Can’t Sleep Until I Find a Rare Glitter Dumpling ” in the style popularised by the world’s most famous YouTuber, Mr Beast. It’s the kind of frantic, shouty, hyper-stimulating unscripted kids’ content shaped in part by an obsessive, second-by-second eye on YouTube Studio’s audience retention graphs. There are a lot of pop-up graphics and fast cuts – a style known as retention editing that has developed specifically around YouTube’s algorithm. Like Mr Beast, Jordan Matter optimises for views with aggressively A/B/C-tested, aggressively colour-saturated thumbnails.
“It’s our responsibility to ensure that we save our kids from this grey matter-destroying nonsense as they won’t do it themselves,” Hooper says. “The strength of the addiction is too strong.”

articles.summary: Sunmi is an undeniable force in K-pop. She first made her debut as a member of the Wonder Girls back in 2007, one of the first K-pop acts to really break through in the West. The English version of their single " Nobody " was the first K-pop song to hit the Billboard Hot 100 in October 2009.
body: Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.

In 2010 Sunmi left the group to go back to school, but the siren call of a music career pulled her back in. She released her debut solo EP Full Moon in 2014. That began a run of award-winning releases for the pop star, including Song of the Year for “Gashina” at the Gaon Chart Music Awards.

Despite her near-constant presence in the K-pop world as a solo artist and as a member of the Wonder Girls, whom she rejoined in 2015, Sumni only just released her first solo LP, Heart Maid, in 2025. This year she released the single “ Forever July,” which blends ’90s R&B synths with rubbery bass and UK garage-inspired drums. Sunmi has called it one of her most personal songs. And she wasn’t afraid to get personal in our Q&A either, revealing details about her writing process, her greatest disappointment as an artist, and her love of ear cleaning videos.

articles.title: The Beautiful Blue Is My Favorite Thing About Vivo’s Foldable X Fold 6
articles.summary: It’s a solid example of an Android foldable, but I worry that Apple has changed the game.
body: Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Having spent a few days with Vivo’s new foldable X Fold 6, I can say there’s plenty I like about it, from its solid camera performance to its extremely good battery life. But because I’m shallow and like pretty things, I have to admit that its vibrant blue design with frosted glass back is my favorite thing about this phone.

It’s by no means the first foldable I’ve liked based on looks alone — Oppo’s Find N6 won me over with its punchy orange color and, like the Oppo, Vivo’s foldable is tough to get hold of. It’s not officially sold in either the US or the UK, and while it’s possible to import these phones from resellers in China or the few parts of Europe where it is sold, I don’t recommend doing so as you’ll be left with no customer support should anything go wrong.

articles.title: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
articles.summary: Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG.
body: Artists are frustrated with the lack of transparency around DistroKid removing their songs.

Musician and self-described “Video Game boy” McGwire reported that six of his songs had been removed from streaming. As has been the case with others, McGwire says that there was no communication from DistroKid before or after the removals, and that he had to contact the company for an explanation.

DistroKid also makes it exceedingly difficult to contact them. McGwire first had to have a “lengthy circular conversation” with a bot before getting hold of a live agent. One of the songs removed was a cover of Stevie Wonder’s “Isn’t She Lovely,” which he claims to have had a proper license for. Another track used a beat he purchased through a marketplace, which others had also licensed.
Most infuriating for McGwire was a song removed for an uncleared sample. The song he allegedly sampled was released two years after his track.
